--- title: "Optimization" description: "Improve the instruction and worked examples a function sends, from your examples, without touching your code." --- Some rules are easy to state: write them in the docstring. Others are easier to show than to say. An optimizer finds what to send the model, besides the inputs, so that it does better on your examples: - the **instruction**, and - the **demos**: worked examples shown before the question. It never edits your code, your types, or the layout. It works in place, and `undo_opt()` goes back. ## Before and after A support desk with house rules the model can't guess: a broken item is a **shipping** claim (the carrier pays), and anything about money back is **billing**. ::: {#3226216b .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} from typing import Literal from dpyr import col @ai def category(message: str) -> Literal["shipping", "billing", "product", "account"]: """The support category of the message.""" dev = [ {"message": "The mug arrived in pieces.", "category": "shipping"}, {"message": "I want my money back for the toaster, it's useless.", "category": "billing"}, {"message": "The kettle's lid doesn't close properly.", "category": "product"}, {"message": "How do I change the email on my profile?", "category": "account"}, {"message": "Box was crushed and the lamp inside is cracked.", "category": "shipping"}, {"message": "Please refund the blender, it stopped working.", "category": "billing"}, {"message": "Toaster burns one side of the bread.", "category": "product"}, {"message": "Screen was shattered when I opened the package.", "category": "shipping"}, {"message": "Return the headphones and give me a refund please.", "category": "billing"}, {"message": "My coupon code didn't apply at checkout.", "category": "billing"}, ] train = [ {"message": "The vase came smashed.", "category": "shipping"}, {"message": "Frying pan arrived with a big dent.", "category": "shipping"}, {"message": "I'd like a refund for the kettle, the lid is loose.", "category": "billing"}, {"message": "Money back please, the chair wobbles.", "category": "billing"}, {"message": "The handle came off after two uses.", "category": "product"}, {"message": "I can't turn on two-factor authentication.", "category": "account"}, ] right = col.pred_result == col.category before = functai.evaluate(category, dev, {"right": right}, num_threads=8) category.opt(trainset=train, metric=right) after = functai.evaluate(category, dev, {"right": right}, num_threads=8) functai.compare(before, after) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: The default optimizer, `BootstrapFewShot`, ran the function on the training rows and kept the runs the metric accepted as demos. What it chose: ::: {#134f08b4 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} for demo in category.demos: print(f"{demo.inputs['message']!r:58} → {demo.outputs['result']}") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 'The handle came off after two uses.' → product "I can't turn on two-factor authentication." → account ``` ::: ::: `category.undo_opt()` reverts; `category.state()` shows the instruction and demos in use; `category.programs()` lists every version optimization produced. ::: {.callout-tip} ## Measure on rows you did not train on Optimize on `trainset`, judge on a separate `dev` set. A score measured on the training rows says how well the demos were memorized, not how well the function works. ::: ## The optimizers | optimizer | what it does | good for | |---|---|---| | `LabeledFewShot(k=16)` | your labeled rows become demos | a quick baseline | | `BootstrapFewShot(...)` (default) | runs the function on training rows; runs the metric accepts become demos, whole turns included (reasoning, tool calls) | most tasks | | `BootstrapFewShotWithRandomSearch(num_candidate_programs=8)` | many demo sets, keeps the best on `valset` | when you have a validation set | | `InstructionSearch(num_candidates=6, num_trials=12)` | a model proposes instructions; each is tried with demo sets on small batches; the best are scored on `valset` | rules that are hard to state | Pass one as `optimizer=`: ::: {#72e15be9 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} from functai import InstructionSearch opt = InstructionSearch(num_candidates=3, num_trials=5, prompt_lm="gpt-4.1-mini") category.opt(trainset=train, valset=dev, metric=right, optimizer=opt) opt.trials # every trial: which instruction, which demos, its score ``` ::: The [translator example](../examples/optimizing_translator.qmd) runs `InstructionSearch` with an AI judge as the metric, before and after. ## Options - **A stronger teacher.** `teacher_lm="gpt-4.1"` (or `teacher=` an AI function) produces the demos, and the cheap model uses them. - **Too few examples?** With a teacher, `n_synth=20` writes training rows first. - **Demos by hand.** `@ai(examples=[("I love it", "positive"), ...])`, as pairs or as rows. - **Keep the result.** `fn.save("category.json")` writes the instruction and demos; `fn.load("category.json")` reads them back. To save the whole program, see [Saving](saving.qmd). ## When optimizing is the wrong tool If you can say the rule in a sentence, say it in the docstring: it is free, readable and exact. Optimizers earn their keep when the rule is hard to put into words and you have examples of it. And if `compare` shows an interval that includes 0, the honest next step is more examples, not more optimizing.
